name: Stout Grove
why: The best wow-per-step grove in the redwoods: the 1929 founding grove of the park, flat and open at the Mill Creek–Smith River confluence, with many trunks over 12 ft thick.
tip: Go early or at dusk when light shafts angle through — and in summer, walk there from the campground over the seasonal footbridge instead of driving.

name: Grove of Titans (via Mill Creek Trail)
why: Some of the largest-volume redwoods known, seen from an elevated boardwalk finished in May 2022. Multi-trunked fusion giants that read as walls of wood.
tip: Park at the marked Grove of Titans lot on Howland Hill Road (ADA parking + restrooms). Stay on the boardwalk — trampled roots are why it had to be built.

name: Boy Scout Tree Trail
why: The park's classic half-day: rooty single-track through dense old growth to the fused double Boy Scout Tree (~2.8 mi in) and little Fern Falls at the end.
tip: Trailhead parking on Howland Hill Road is small — claim it before mid-morning in summer.

name: Mill Creek Trail
why: A quieter creek-side walk through the forest between Howland Hill Road and the river — the long way to the Titans, with varied thrush and Pacific wren for company.
tip: Combine with Stout Grove: the north end comes out near the grove.

name: Simpson-Reed & Peterson Loop
why: Old growth without the drive down Howland Hill: a lush, ferny, sorrel-floored loop right off US-199, heavy with hemlocks growing out of nurse logs.
tip: Best quick redwood fix if you're arriving late or leaving early — trailhead off 199/Walker Rd.

name: Leiffer & Ellsworth Loops
why: The solitude option: less-visited loops near Walker Road with a creek crossing and the same giant trees, minus the crowds.
tip: Pairs naturally with Simpson-Reed across the way.

name: Hiouchi Trail
why: River's-edge old growth on the south bank: fern grottoes, river views, and in summer a direct link over the footbridge to Stout Grove.
tip: Start near the Hiouchi Bridge (US-199 side) and walk upriver; watch for otters in the pools below.

name: Hatton Trail & Loop
why: A quiet connector through big trees on the north side of US-199 — the short loop is an easy leg-stretcher; the full trail links toward the river trails.
tip: Trailhead pullout is on US-199 just west of Hiouchi — easy to miss, worth the U-turn.

name: Little Bald Hills Trail
why: The strangest transition in the park: climb out of the tallest forest on Earth onto open serpentine barrens with stunted pines and rare wildflowers. Spring is spectacular.
tip: Read the serpentine section of the Field Guide first — the 'why' makes the climb. Water: there's little up top.

name: Howland Hill Road (scenic drive)
stats: ~6 mi unpaved · 30–45 min · no RVs or trailers
why: A one-lane 1887 county road that never got modernized — which is why you can now drive slowly through cathedral old growth with trunks at your mirrors.
tip: Pull well into pullouts for oncoming cars. It's the 1887 free road of the history report — not an 1850s stage route, whatever the guidebooks say.

name: Summer footbridge & River Beach
why: Roughly July–September (river level permitting), the seasonal footbridge below the campground links straight to Stout Grove — and the gravel-bar beaches on the way are the park's swimming holes.
tip: Water is cold and clearer than it looks — deeper too. No lifeguards; keep kids in the calm side channels.

name: Battery Point Lighthouse
why: An 1856 lighthouse (first lit December 1856) on a tidal islet you walk to across the rocks — one of the oldest lights on the Pacific coast, with a keeper's-house museum run by the county historical society.
tip: Crossable only around low tide and it floods fast — check a Crescent City tide table before you commit, and give yourself the return window.

name: Brother Jonathan Cemetery & Vista Point
why: The bluff-top memorial to the 1865 wreck that killed over 200 people — the deadliest Pacific coast shipwreck of its day (the full story is on the Historical Map). Sweeping ocean panorama.
tip: Pair with Pebble Beach Drive just below for the sunset run home.

name: Harbor sea lions & Marine Mammal Center
why: California sea lions haul out and argue on the harbor docks year-round; the volunteer-run Northcoast Marine Mammal Center next door rehabs rescued seals and sea lions (donation-based, kids love it).
tip: Bring binoculars for harbor seals — the quieter, spotted ones lounging apart from the noisy sea lions.

name: Point St. George
why: Wide, wild headland with grassy bluff paths, tidepools below, and the St. George Reef Lighthouse on the horizon — the ocean grandstand: gray whales Dec–Jan and Mar–May, seabirds always.
tip: Windbreaker mandatory. The 1892 lighthouse offshore is the one built after the Brother Jonathan wreck — binoculars make the connection.

name: Pebble Beach Drive
why: Sea stacks, surf, and pullouts the whole way between Crescent City and Point St. George — the local sunset route.
tip: Evening light on the offshore rocks is the show; any pullout works.

name: Tolowa Dunes SP & Lake Earl
why: A huge dune-and-lagoon wilderness — one of California's largest coastal lagoon systems — loud with waterfowl in winter and busy with raptors year-round. Also storied Tolowa ground: Yontocket stands at its north edge (see the Historical Map), so walk as a guest.
tip: Trails can be soft sand or seasonal mud; birders should hit the Lake Earl overlooks off Lake Earl Drive at first light.

name: Beachfront Park & B Street Pier
why: The easy town stop: harbor-front park with the big KidTown playground, plus the public fishing pier for sunset, sea lions, and pelicans.
tip: Rainy-day rotation: pier walk, then Rumiano Cheese's shop (family creamery since 1919) ten blocks up.

name: Crescent Beach Overlook & Enderts Beach
why: The most accessible great tidepools in the park complex: a short trail drops from the overlook to a rocky cove where low tide opens the whole zonation — stars, anemones, chitons.
tip: Time it to arrive an hour before a good low tide; the Field Guide's tidepool page is written for exactly this spot.

name: Damnation Creek Trail
stats: ~4 mi round trip · strenuous (1,100 ft down & back up)
why: The redwoods-to-the-sea hike: down an old-growth canyon on the historic highway grade to a wild rocky cove. The fog-forest descent is as atmospheric as this coast gets.
tip: Remember the elevation is all on the way back — save water and daylight for the climb. Trailhead pullout on US-101 fills; go early.

name: Yurok Loop & Hidden Beach
why: A gentle coastal-bluff loop from Lagoon Creek through wildflower scrub to driftwood-piled Hidden Beach — huge views, tiny effort.
tip: Combine with False Klamath Cove's roadside beach just north for a two-stop coast morning.

name: Klamath River Overlook
stats: ~40 min drive · short walk from parking
why: A 600-ft bluff over the Klamath's meeting with the Pacific — the celebrated whale-watching stand on this coast, with sea lions working the river mouth below.
tip: Dec–Jan and Mar–May for gray whales; take the lower overlook spur if your knees agree.

name: Trees of Mystery
why: The classic roadside stop done well: a gondola through the redwood canopy, carved-tree trails, the giant Paul Bunyan — and the End of the Trail museum's genuinely significant Native American collection (free with admission).
tip: The SkyTrail gondola is the part worth the ticket — canopy level is a different forest.

name: Fern Canyon & Elk Meadow (Prairie Creek)
why: A slot canyon walled floor-to-rim in ferns (yes, the Jurassic Park one), plus near-guaranteed Roosevelt elk at Elk Meadow on the way in.
tip: Summer gatekeeping is real: a free day-use permit is required May 15–Sep 15 (book ahead on the state-parks site), and Davison Road bars trailers/large RVs. Elk are wild — 100 ft minimum.

name: Myrtle Creek Botanical Trail
why: An 1850s mining-ditch grade turned botanical walk where serpentine chemistry flips the flora — including pitcher-plant seeps. Five minutes from Hiouchi.
tip: Trailhead pullout on US-199 just east of the park at the Myrtle Creek bridge; the ditch story is in the history report's road section.

name: Pitcher-plant fens (Smith River NRA)
why: Knee-high cobra-hooded Darlingtonia in wet serpentine seeps — carnivorous plants at highway distance.
tip: Ask at the Gasquet ranger station (US-199) for the current best fen stop; Myrtle Creek and Little Bald Hills have them too.

name: The Forks — river swimming
why: Where the Middle and South Forks meet to make the mainstem: deep green pools, gravel beaches, and summer swimming the Smith is famous for.
tip: Local access points vary — the park's own River Beach and Panther Flat (below) are the reliable, signed options. Cold water, real current, no lifeguards.

name: Panther Flat day-use & swimming
stats: ~25 min drive · signed Forest Service site
why: The dependable upriver swimming hole: easy pull-off on US-199 by Panther Flat campground, gravel banks into clear Middle Fork pools.
tip: Even in a heat wave the water is snowmelt-cold — glorious for ten minutes at a time.

name: Gasquet & the ranger station
why: The little Six Rivers gateway town: gas, general store, and the Smith River NRA ranger station — the people to ask about fens, forest roads, and foraging rules.
tip: Last services before the Oregon mountains if you're continuing up 199.

name: Crissey Field Welcome Center (OR)
why: Dunes and beach at the Winchuck River's mouth on the state line — the very place Jedediah Smith's party camped entering Oregon on June 23, 1828 (pin on the Historical Map).
tip: The Oregon welcome center has good maps and clean restrooms; the beach walk south reaches the river mouth.
